metadata.title: Overrepresentation of female teachers in secondary education and gender achievement gaps in PISA 2022

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 achievement data aggregated to the country level (gender gaps computed as female mean minus male mean) and merges these with UNESCO/ILOSTAT indicators of female teacher shares and female labor-force participation. Because the analysis is explicitly country-level (65 countries) and focuses on bivariate and multiple regression with country-level aggregates, the paper does not apply PISA student sampling weights in the usual microdata sense. Instead, it reports two weighting perspectives: unweighted analyses where each country contributes equally, and weighted analyses where countries are weighted by the number of 15-year-olds represented in PISA (population-size weights), with results shown to differ (weighted analyses yield stronger correlations). The manuscript therefore treats weighting as an aggregation/population-representation adjustment rather than a replicate-weighted complex survey estimation; no replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are country-level gender achievement gaps computed from PISA 2022 average male and female scores (female minus male), and the paper does not describe plausible-value (PV) generation/combining or PV-based uncertainty propagation at the country-gap level. Missing-data handling is also not reported as a specific imputation/deletion rule; the paper only states that 16 countries were excluded due to missing data on the female teacher share and/or female labor-force participation. This means the missing-data strategy is only partially documented (country exclusion), while the treatment of missingness within PISA-derived inputs is not specified.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study analyzes PISA 2022 country-level data for 65 countries that participated in PISA 2022. Of the 81 participating countries and economies, 16 were excluded because of missing data on either (a) the percentage of female teachers in secondary education (UNESCO Institute for Statistics) and/or (b) the percentage of female workers in the national labor force (ILOSTAT). The paper also notes a special data handling case for Cyprus: PISA data for Cyprus were downloaded from the PISA National Center Cyprus website because Cyprus was not included in the international PISA dataset. For the country-level gender achievement gaps, the outcome is computed as the difference between each country’s average female and average male scores in reading, mathematics, and science.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Reading (15-year-olds, country-level gender gap female minus male)
main_findings.target_variable: Gender achievement gap in reading (female advantage)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Bivariate (unweighted): β=0.611, R²=0.317, p<.001; Bivariate (weighted): β=0.749, R²=0.515, p<.001. Multiple regression (unweighted): overrepresentation β=0.475, p<.001, R²=0.371. Multiple regression (weighted): overrepresentation β=0.659, p<.001, R²=0.564.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Reading data aggregated to country-level gender gaps, the study leveraged Overrepresentation of female teachers (and, secondarily, Students in single-sex schools and family-support-related controls) to predict the female–male achievement gap in reading, finding that higher female overrepresentation in secondary teaching is associated with larger female advantages. This indicates that policies affecting the gender composition of the teaching workforce may be linked to cross-national differences in gendered academic outcomes, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics (15-year-olds, country-level gender gap female minus male)
main_findings.target_variable: Gender achievement gap in mathematics (male advantage)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Bivariate (unweighted): β=0.481, R²=0.231, p<.001; Bivariate (weighted): β=0.838, R²=0.398, p<.001. Multiple regression (unweighted): overrepresentation β=0.336, p=.002, R²=0.490. Multiple regression (weighted): overrepresentation β=0.265, p<.001, R²=0.780.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics data aggregated to country-level gender gaps, the study leveraged Overrepresentation of female teachers (with additional selected controls such as family-support and working-for-pay gender differences) to predict the female–male achievement gap in mathematics, finding that greater female overrepresentation is associated with a smaller female disadvantage (i.e., a reduced male advantage). This indicates that workforce-gender composition may relate to narrowing gender achievement gaps in mathematics, but causality cannot be inferred from these country-level correlations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Science (15-year-olds, country-level gender gap female minus male)
main_findings.target_variable: Gender achievement gap in science (female advantage)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Bivariate (unweighted): β=0.533, R²=0.284, p<.001; Bivariate (weighted): β=0.866, R²=0.505, p<.001. Multiple regression (unweighted): overrepresentation β=0.317, p=.006, R²=0.432. Multiple regression (weighted): overrepresentation β=0.550, p<.001, R²=0.651.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Science data aggregated to country-level gender gaps, the study leveraged Overrepresentation of female teachers (with robustness checks including selected country-level controls) to predict the female–male achievement gap in science, finding that higher female overrepresentation is associated with larger female advantages. This indicates that teacher workforce gender composition may be a meaningful correlate of gendered science achievement patterns, while the cross-sectional, country-aggregate approach limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 country-level achievement data for 65 participating countries, computing gender achievement gaps as the difference between average female and male scores in reading, mathematics, and science. It merges these gaps with UNESCO (female teacher shares in secondary education) and ILOSTAT (female labor-force participation) and defines an overrepresentation index as the difference between female teacher share and female labor-force share. Across bivariate and multiple regression models, the overrepresentation of female teachers is the only predictor that consistently shows robust association with gender achievement gaps in all three subjects. In bivariate analyses, the weighted correlations are strongest for science (β=0.711, R²=0.505) and mathematics (β=0.631, R²=0.398), while multiple regression shows substantial model fit (R²=0.564 reading; 0.780 mathematics; 0.651 science). The paper reports no PV-handling or missing-data imputation strategy; it excludes 16 countries with missing UNESCO/ILOSTAT inputs, and the cross-sectional design precludes causal claims.
